paper_source: Publisher PDF (emailed-pdf provenance) staged in the private papers repository as the Issue 138 bundle; doi 10.1038/s41598-023-43152-4
show_notes:
**[Seasonal variations of functional connectivity of human brains](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-43152-4)**

*Scientific Reports, 2023*

DOI: [10.1038/s41598-023-43152-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-43152-4)

**Question:** Does resting-state fMRI activity and connectivity differ with the season in which a person is scanned?

**Answer:** In 410 Human Connectome Project adults, each measured at one time of year, low-frequency signal power (fALFF) and some connectivity measures peaked in autumn. Global connectivity failed its omnibus test, no multiple-comparison correction is reported, and scanner stability was unchecked.

**Three takeaways**

1. fALFF differed by season in grey and white matter (p = 0.013 and 0.017), highest in autumn.
2. Global GM-WM connectivity was not significant overall (p = 0.089); 3 of 14 networks passed, uncorrected, at most about 20% above their lowest season.
3. The pattern leans on one high autumn quarter more than a smooth cycle, and the authors could not check scanner calibration.
verification_changes: Nadia said autumn was about twenty percent above the lowest season in all three significant networks; the paper says the highest was approximately 20% above the lowest, and Fig. 5 shows about 20-22% for ventral DMN and posterior insula but about 14% for sensorimotor. Restated as the top of the range, here and in show-notes takeaway 2.

Nadia said on almost every plot winter, spring and summer sit flat and autumn alone sticks up; Figs. 1 and 6 show a summer dip in WM fALFF, density and transitivity (winter vs summer transitivity is significant). Limited the flat-then-autumn shape to the connectivity plots, and softened takeaway 3 (dialogue and show notes) from 'one odd quarter rather than a smooth cycle' to 'leans on one high autumn quarter', since fALFF and three WM graph properties did pass the sinusoid test.

Nadia said a three-parameter sine fit to four means 'will always look tidy'; the fit has one residual degree of freedom and did fail for global FC and the three networks. Restated as a weak test rather than a guaranteed pass.
Turn 7 said white-matter signal 'used to be treated as noise'; the paper never says so. Replaced with the paper's own statement that cited work links WM BOLD signal to neural activity.
Turn 12 said each person was scanned 'over a day or two'; the paper does not state the scan schedule. Cut.
Turn 22 said grey matter 'doesn't show' the graph-property shift; the paper says GM-GM was not significant but similar trends were observed. Added the authors' caveat.

Theo asked for the sexes to be tested against each other as though the paper had not compared them; it reports a significant male-female difference in winter (Supp. Fig. S6). Added that, and reframed the ask as comparing the seasonal contrast between sexes.

Turn 36 stated the HCP recruited twins and siblings, which this paper never says. Verified against Van Essen et al. 2013, NeuroImage (the HCP overview, PMC3724347: subjects 'drawn from a population of adult twins and their non-twin siblings') and attributed to the project's own description.

Theo said the environmental fit was easy 'once you allow a lag'; the regression modelled no lag (the lag was an observation). Reworded to the freedom two seasonal regressors give over four time points.

Episode ninety-four callback said the authors ran 'cross-sectional' comparisons and that it was 'exactly' this paper's comparison, under 'this design problem twice before'; card 094 says standard non-experimental designs, and episode thirty-four is a contrast, not the same problem. Reworded to the card and softened.
Turn 44 said 'nothing is corrected'; the paper only fails to report a correction. Changed to 'no correction is reported'.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hello, and welcome to Science TLDR. I'm Nadia.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And I'm Theo. Today it's a question I've half-wondered about every time I've sat in a scanner in January.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Whether your brain is a different brain depending on the season. The paper is called Seasonal variations of functional connectivity of human brains, from a group at Vanderbilt, in Scientific Reports. The short version: they took resting brain scans from about four hundred young adults, sorted them by the season each person was scanned in, and report that several measures of brain activity peak in autumn.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So why is this worth ten minutes? Seasonal mood effects are old news. What does this add, and who should care?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Two groups. Anyone curious whether the seasonal patterns in mood and cognition show up in the brain's own signals. And, more practically, anyone who runs imaging studies over months. If the season moves these measures, it's a confound nobody records. That second audience is the one I'd take seriously.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay. Then set up the measurement for me, because resting-state imaging gets talked about as if everyone knows what it measures.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Right. Functional M-R-I tracks a blood-oxygen signal that rises and falls with local activity. At rest, with no task, those signals drift slowly, and regions that drift together are called functionally connected. They measured two things. One is how much of each region's signal sits in those slow fluctuations, with the unfortunate name fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations. I'll just call it slow-wave power. The other is connectivity: how tightly regions correlate.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Um, and one unusual choice: they include white matter, the wiring, and correlate it against grey matter. The authors cite earlier work suggesting the white-matter signal tracks neural activity too.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Fine. And the data?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The Human Connectome Project, a large public dataset. They kept four hundred ten people in a narrow age band, healthy adults in their late twenties and early thirties, scanned over two years.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Those are binned into four seasons of roughly a hundred people each. The central claim, in one sentence: resting brain activity varies with the season, and it's highest in autumn.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Hold on, because the design matters more than any result here. Those are four different groups of people. Nobody was followed through the year. So the claim that a brain changes with the seasons is being made from a comparison between strangers. Is that a fair description?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It's exact. Every person is measured at a single point in the year. Whatever the paper says about variation, it's variation between the people who happened to come in during autumn and the people who came in during summer.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Then let's see what the comparison shows. Start with the strongest result.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Slow-wave power. In both grey and white matter, it differs across the four seasons, and that test is reasonably clear of chance. It drifts down from winter to summer and then jumps up in autumn. The autumn-versus-summer gap is the biggest, and it's a moderate effect by the usual yardsticks rather than a tiny one.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: A moderate gap between groups of a hundred is not nothing. What happens with connectivity, which is the word in the title?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hmm. Weaker. The overall test across all four seasons doesn't reach significance. They then compare pairs of seasons anyway, and autumn comes out above the other three, by about a tenth. And when they try to fit a smooth yearly cycle to it, the fit fails.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Oh — so the headline measure in the title fails its own omnibus test, and the significance arrives afterwards in the pairwise comparisons. That's the order of operations a reviewer flags first.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It is. Then they break connectivity into fourteen brain networks. Three of them show a seasonal difference: a sensorimotor network, part of the default mode network, which is the set of regions active when you're not doing anything in particular, and the posterior insula. The authors put the highest season at about twenty percent above the lowest. Reading the plots, that's the top of the range; the sensorimotor gap is smaller.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Three of fourteen. Let me lay out the two readings. In one, these three networks are where the season actually acts, and the twenty percent is real. In the other, you ran fourteen tests at the usual threshold, and some will pass by luck. Do they correct for the number of tests?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Uh, the paper doesn't report any correction. Not for the fourteen networks, not across the dozens of tests overall. And the effect sizes they do report are small by the usual conventions. The three networks also fail the test for a smooth yearly cycle.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Mm. So I can't tell those two readings apart on this paper. I'm not saying the three networks are noise. I'm saying nothing here distinguishes them from it.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's fair. There's one more set of results, which I find the most interesting. They treat the brain as a graph, regions as nodes and strong correlations as links, and compute things like how densely linked it is and how short the paths are between regions. For white matter to white matter, every one of those properties shifts with season, and the autumn network is denser and more efficient. Grey matter doesn't reach significance, though the authors say the trend looks similar.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Why white matter alone? That seems like either the real story or a warning sign.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Well... they don't really explain it. And that's where I'd want to look at the plots, because the figures tell you something the text doesn't. On the connectivity plots, winter, spring and summer sit close together, nearly flat, and autumn alone sticks up. Some of the others have a summer dip too, but autumn is the extreme on every one.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And it's worth knowing what autumn means here. The seasons follow the dataset's acquisition quarters, so autumn runs from August through October, and winter from November through January.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So their autumn starts in high summer. That's worth holding onto when we get to the weather.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Back to the shape, though.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Huh. That's a different shape from the one the paper describes. A sine wave is a smooth tide. What you're describing, at least for connectivity, is one quarter that's out of line with the other three. Those suggest very different causes.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Yes. And the sine-wave fitting doesn't settle it. There are four time points, one per season, and the fit has an amplitude, a phase and an offset. Three free numbers to describe four averages. That leaves the fit very little room to fail, so passing it is a weak test of a yearly cycle.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: To their credit, they flag part of this themselves. They note that a sine wave is symmetrical, so it may not be the right shape, and that they lacked exact scan dates, so each season is treated as one time point. They say a different curve would give similar conclusions, but they don't show it.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So let me take the room on the alternative. If one quarter of acquisitions differs, I want to know what else differed in that quarter. A scanner drifts. Software gets updated. The staff changes. Recruitment shifts. Did they check the instrument?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: They say plainly that they couldn't. Scanner calibration data weren't available, and they state that as a limitation, which is to their credit. And the methods drop the earliest quarters of the dataset because those were reconstructed with an older algorithm, so the pipeline did change over the project's life.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Then how do they argue the scanner out of it?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Two arguments. The measures are normalized, and the effect isn't uniform across the brain. And when they split by sex, women show a seasonal difference and men don't, and the sexes differ from each other in winter. They say this sex-dependent pattern has basically ruled out the scanner.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: I don't think it does. Men are the smaller group here, so missing a significant difference in them is weak evidence of anything. And a scanner artifact doesn't have to treat every brain identically. A difference in significance isn't a significant difference, and a gap in one season isn't a different seasonal pattern. I'd want the seasonal contrast itself compared between the sexes.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Mm-hm. I'd add one they don't mention. The Connectome Project's own description says it recruited twins and their siblings, and this paper doesn't say how relatives were handled. If related people were scanned in the same season, the groups are less independent than a hundred people each suggests.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Now the weather. The abstract says temperature and daylength may explain how this arises. What's behind that?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: They took average temperature and daylength for St. Louis, where the scans were done, and used them as regressors. They predict slow-wave power. They don't predict connectivity. And the peaks don't line up: temperature and daylength peak in summer, slow-wave power peaks in autumn.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Then that's carrying more than the data can. With four time points, two seasonal regressors have plenty of freedom to fit anything else seasonal. That's city-wide weather standing in for whatever each person was exposed to. I'd call it consistent with an environmental story, not evidence for one.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Agreed. And to be fair, they frame the lag as an observation, not a mechanism. Where I'd push back harder is the discussion. They suggest the seasonal swings can be as large as those from many neurological conditions, and they propose these networks as targets for treating seasonal affective disorder.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Neither is in the data. Nobody here had a mood measure, nobody had a diagnosis, and no comparison to a neurological condition is shown. That's a leap from a between-group difference in healthy young adults.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Yeah, that's speculation, and it's the part I'd ignore.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: We've seen what this kind of design can cost. In episode ninety-four, the social media deactivation study, the authors ran standard non-experimental comparisons on their own randomized data, and the estimates came out biased in unpredictable directions, sometimes the wrong sign. That's the same broad kind of comparison this paper rests on.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And it's a nice contrast with episode thirty-four, the consciousness adversarial collaboration, also imaging. There, the analyses were preregistered before anyone saw data. Here, a lot of tests are run, the passes are reported, and no correction is reported. Same kind of scanner, very different discipline.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So here's my verdict, and it's narrow. This doesn't establish that any person's brain cycles with the seasons. It's an uncorrected, between-group warning that scan date might be a confound in imaging studies. As a warning, I'll take it, because recording the date costs nothing.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: I'd put it slightly more kindly. They used public data, named the scanner problem themselves, and the slow-wave power result is the cleanest thing here. It's a reasonable reason for the next long study to log the season. That's what it earns.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Then three takeaways. One: across about four hundred people, slow-wave brain power differed by season, highest in autumn, and that's the paper's firmest result. Two: connectivity failed the overall test, and three of fourteen networks passing uncorrected tells you very little. Three: the pattern leans on one high autumn quarter more than a smooth cycle, and nobody could check the scanner.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: What I'd watch for is the same people scanned across a year. If autumn still stands out within a person, I'll believe the brain is doing it.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And I'd watch for anyone with a calibrated scanner and a phantom scan every week. If the autumn bump shows up in the phantom too, the story's over. If it doesn't, I'd take this a lot more seriously.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The paper is in Scientific Reports, twenty twenty-three. Thanks for listening to Science TLDR.
